newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian economy headed for lower 1996/97 growth.
newsitem.headline: Indian economy headed for lower 1996/97 growth.

text.p: India'a economy is heading for a slowdown in fiscal 1996/97 (April-March), largely due to high interest rates in the second half of 1995/96 that led industry to cut back on investments, economists and analysts said on Friday.
They said a severe liquidity crunch in the second half of 1995/96 led to high nominal interest rates, with some banks charging as high as 19 percent per annum.

"Investments are not viable at such rates," said the chairman of a state-run bank, who declined to be named. "The high cost led to postponement of investments. We are now seeing the impact of last year's high interest rates."

On Thursday, India's largest commercial bank, the State Bank of India (SBI) said it was cutting its prime lending rate to 15.5 percent per annum from 16 percent in a bid to revive demand for bank credit.

"The prime lending rate will be cut further in case the credit offtake does not increase despite the commencement of the busy season this month," SBI chairman Kakodkar was quoted by the Business Standard newspaper as saying.
India's year-on-year growth rate in gross domestic product was 6.3 percent in 1994/95, and seven percent in 1995/96.
"As of now, it looks as if last year's growth cannot be repeated," said R.H. Patil, managing director of India's National Stock Exchange.
Analysts based their forecast on the rate of growth of bank credit, imports and industrial production, all of which point to a slowdown.

As of August 16, 1996, bank credit was 2,678.05 billion rupees ($74.9 billion), down 18.02 billion rupees from that at the end of fiscal 1995/96, according to the Reserve Bank of India. Bank credit grew by 2.92 billion rupees in the same period last year.
"The fall in bank credit is a clear indication that industry is slowing down," an analyst said.

Said Sanjeev Sanyal, economist at Crosby Ltd: "we expect the Indian economy to grow at around 6.1 percent in 1996/97. Non-oil imports have slowed down, showing that industrial production is slackening."

The Centre for Monitoring the Indian Economy, an independent Bombay-based research firm, said non-oil imports rose only seven percent during April-June 1996 against a 41 percent rise in the year-ago period.
"We expect industrial production to be about 8.0-9.0 percent (higher) this year against more than 12 percent last year," Sanyal said.

The government's index of production showed the year-on-year industrial production growth rate slowing right from the start of calendar 1996. The rate fell to 9.8 percent in March and to 7.4 percent in April from 13.1 percent in February.
